Title: RIFT-Bench: Dynamic Red-teaming For Agentic AI Systems
Abstract: Agentic AI systems powered by large language models (LLMs) are rapidly evolving into autonomous decision-making systems, exposing attack vectors beyond those of traditional LLM vulnerabilities. Existing security evaluations are often tied to specific implementations or domains, limiting unified comparison across heterogeneous systems. To address this gap, we introduce RIFT-Bench, a representation-driven methodology for dynamic red-teaming that enables unified evaluations across diverse agentic architectures. Building on a novel hierarchical representation, RIFT-Bench operates in two automated phases: Discovery, which extracts system structure, and Scanning, which executes adaptive adversarial attacks. It directly evaluates the examined system using 105 adaptive adversarial probes spanning diverse attack vectors and objectives. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed evaluation pipeline across 45 agentic systems spanning a diverse range of implementations, showing that the approach generalizes effectively to heterogeneous agentic architectures. Beyond systems and attacks, RIFT-Bench also supports direct evaluation of mitigation strategies. These key capabilities make RIFT-Bench a scalable foundation for security evaluation of agentic AI systems in practice. Infrastructure code and benchmark artifacts are available at https://github.com/ FujitsuResearch/RIFT-Bench.where each component corresponds to a node with metadata and can recursively contain other nodes, capturing both local components and higher-level system structure. NodeSpec provides a unified representation of agentic systems and is designed to support systematic modification of system components across heterogeneous implementations. Each node is characterized along five dimensions:• Identity: core identifiers such as node name and type.• Provenance: links to implementation artifacts, including code references and descriptive context.• Topology: structural relationships, including child components and connectivity.• Interface and configuration: inputs, outputs, prompts, and required resources.• Capabilities: behavioral properties such as code execution and data-access permissions. Appendix D provides the full field list and a detailed NodeSpec example. A key design principle of NodeSpec is that it is implementation-grounded. Code references, prompts, and configuration values preserve direct links to the system implementation. This enables adaptation and controlled manipulation of specific system components. RIFT-Bench: MethodologyRIFT-Bench operates in two phases, as illustrated in Fig. 1. First, Discovery analyzes the system implementation and generates a code-driven representation (NodeSpec). Based on this representation, the Scanning phase adaptively selects and instantiates applicable adversarial probes as attack attempts tailored to the examined system. The system's behavior is then evaluated from the resulting execution traces. Together, these phases enable scalable and systematic evaluation of both agentic systems and adversarial probes. Discovery PhaseThis phase extracts the agentic system structure and prepares it for safe, scalable evaluation. The structure identifier (SI) analyzes the system code to derive its NodeSpec representation, after which configurable tool emulation is integrated to support safe and cost-aware execution. Major_Contribution_Result: RIFT-Bench is a representation-driven dynamic red-teaming methodology for heterogeneous agentic systems: a Discovery phase extracts a NodeSpec hierarchical structure (with optional tool emulation), and a Scanning phase runs adaptive adversarial probes. The benchmark uses 105 adaptive probes and is demonstrated on 45 agentic systems spanning diverse implementations, also supporting evaluation of mitigation strategies. Scanning reports metrics including Attack Activation Rate, conditional/total ASR, mean execution drift, and utility where available.
Research_Limitations_Challenges: The authors state RIFT-Bench is white-box and assumes access to implementation code; gray/black-box auditing is left as complementary future work. It currently depends on an existing tracing stack (e.g., MLflow). Scope is text-based agentic systems, not multimodal agents/attack surfaces. The probe set is broad but not exhaustive. Future work includes more granular analysis of how evaluator choice affects vulnerability conclusions.
Critics: This is a system-level evaluation/red-teaming infrastructure paper rather than a single new attack or defense algorithm. Its value for LLM-agent security evaluation is unified scanning across heterogeneous implementations; reported vulnerability patterns remain probe-, system-, and evaluator-dependent. It does not by itself provide a complete mitigation–reassessment release gate, and white-box/code-access assumptions limit direct transfer to closed deployments.
